subsubtopic: PROPOSED PROGRAM FOR ECONOMIC RECONSTRUCTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I rise to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In the light of the continuing evidence of economic disarray in our country confirmed by today's CPI statement, and of the urgent need for leadership to halt our economic destruction, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey):
That this House calls upon the government to begin immediately a program of economic reconstruction which shall include the following:
(1)	A commitment to stable monetary policy.
(2)	A commitment to increase the relative size of the productive element of the economy, i.e. the private sector.
(3)	A cut in the federal sales tax on building supplies to stimulate demand for housing and thus create jobs in the construction industry.
(4)	An emergency job creation program.
(5)	Long term tax incentives for firms investing in Atlantic Canada or Quebec.
(6)	Specific tax assistance to encourage small and medium-sized businesses, and
(7)	A new budget.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 prompted by the urgent necessity of turning around this government's so-called anti-inflation policies before the social and economic fabric of our country suffers further irreparable harm.
Believing that Canadians cannot for much longer tolerate policies which use mass unemployment to fight inflation, print money at record rates to fight mass unemployment and, finally, blame the private sector, which must live with the
results of government mismanagement on this colossal scale for not investing more in permanent job creation, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House deplores the government's record of nine years of economic failure and calls for an immediate program of economic reconstruction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to move a motion seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
In view of the escalating cost of living as reflected in this month's increase in the CPI of 0.7 per cent which brings the increase for the first six months of 1977 to almost 5 per cent, and in view of the coming increases in oil and natural gas prices, which will lead to another significant increase in the cost of living so that the increase for 1977 is expected to be between 9 per cent and 10 per cent, and whereas wage and salary increases for this year have been limited to 6 per cent, I wish to move:
That this House condemns the government policies which will mean a reduced standard of living in 1977 for most Canadians.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, I should like to direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. In an interjection on June 13 when I was speaking in the House, the Minister of Finance said that he had had private indications from the Canadian Labour Congress that they were prepared to cooperate toward participation in a multipartite national forum which the minister put forward some months ago. Can the minister tell the House whether there have been private talks between the CLC and cabinet ministers which indicate that they are prepared to participate in the multipartite national forum or is the position of the CLC as it has been publicly stated, namely that they are not prepared to participate in that particular forum.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: POSITION OF CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS ON PARTICIPATION IN MULTIPARTITE NATIONAL FORUM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the position can be more accurately stated to be this. Discussions with the CLC with reference to the multipartite forum and other various types of institutions that would ensure a working together between government, labour and business are all part of the discussions that surround an acceptable formula for decontrol. These discussions are still going on. There is no conclusion with respect to them.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: POSITION OF CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS ON PARTICIPATION IN MULTIPARTITE NATIONAL FORUM
speechtext:
My question is whether the Minister of Finance is correct when he says he has had private communications which are contrary to what the CLC has been saying publicly.
I would like the minister to answer that. As well, will he advise whether he realizes that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association as recently as yesterday said that they view this multipartite national forum as just "window dressing". If that is their understanding on the position of labour, the minister ought to inform the House whether in view of the fact that neither management nor labour will support that particular proposition, how long this government is going to hold it out as policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a very worthwhile proposal indeed, one that merits support. I think the hon. member will agree with that. This is a very worth while proposal indeed and is one which merits support. I think the hon. member would agree. subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS

speechtext:
Now wait a minute!
July 13, 1977

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: POSITION OF CANADIAN LABOUR CONGRESS ON PARTICIPATION IN MULTIPARTITE NATIONAL FORUM
speechtext: If you don't mind, I am answering the question. You wait a minute until I am finished, then you can ask another question. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association may not be reflecting the encouraging words we have heard from many in the business community. It is not the only spokesman for the business community. There are many in the business community who have been involved in discussions with reference to the multipartite approach. Labour wants to have a voice, as has often been stated, within a national forum where it can have some influence in the development of national economic policies. This affords them such an opportunity. The fact that they may want to negotiate with respect to the characteristics of such a council seems to me to be quite reasonable and acceptable, and a discussion of that sort is going on in the context, as I say, of talks with reference to decontrol.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS

speechtext: A representative of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Sydney Jackson, said yesterday as reported in the press today: "My view and the view of any business leaders I have talked to is that this would be window dressing and a waste of time. speechtext: Am I supposed to believe the Minister of Finance?

speechtext: The other false premise is that Mr. Jackson speaks for the labour movement, or speaks to it on any regular basis. I do not believe he does-certainly not on a more regular basis than I have been doing myself for some time with respect to this item.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last night before the adjournment, I was wondering why this same government was again anxious to discourage tourist-hunters by requiring-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Order, please. I wonder if hon. members who wish to leave the chamber would do so promptly in order that the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) may continue.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying last night before the adjournment, I am wondering why this same government is still anxious to discourage tourist-hunters who come to my constituency where hunting is the favourite sport of many people, to spend their money to buy ammunition, rifles, and so forth. This government wants to impose- and I do not know if we may call it a tax, but I am inclined to call it so-or require small businesses to pay between $10 and $200 for selling guns and ammunition.
That is why I say the government wants to discourage small business because, instead of bringing all the necessary ammunition and food for one or two weeks vacation in our Canadian forests, we know that these tourists do not go into these small businesses or stores only to buy ammunition, but they also buy their food and all they need.
One might also wonder who will again benefit from stopping sales by the small retailer who surely will not be interested in paying again for another permit, since he is already paying for one to the provincial government, and he will not be interested in continuing to sell the small stock he owns to help hunters get ammunition, so who will benefit from that? As the minister stated it so well yesterday, asking $250 will encourage companies like Eaton's and Simpsons. For them indeed $250 will be something minimal, whereas our small industries and retailers will have to pay $10, $15 or even $25 perhaps only to sell, as I said, $50 worth of merchandise.
My party and I believe that we have to support the motion put forward by the Progressive Conservative Party to the effect that the government should withdraw that permit obligation for small businesses. In conclusion, I urge the government to consider carefully that possibility if they do not want small businesses to close their doors; they should help them by not having them take a permit to sell ammunition and a few long guns during that wonderful time the hunting season is for many people.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate very briefly in the debate on this motion by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). First of all, I should point out that I am in support of the motion. The thrust of these particular clauses of Bill C-51 is simply tantamount to another form of taxation as it relates to the individual and as it relates to the business entrepreneur. It is simply another cost of doing business.
It is very strange that we have a Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand) going around the country boasting about the measures the Liberal government has engaged in, in terms of improving the climate and the environment of small business enterprises in Canada. He has talked about removing bureaucratic red tape and the number of forms and statistics which have been burdened on small business. Yet here we have another example of bureaucratic intervention, another form of taxation and another cost item which will do nothing in terms of preventing crime. How will the imposition of a fee for an
July 13, 1977

individual to acquire a firearm or a permit, or for a business enterprise to engage in the sale of firearms, in any way assist in stamping out crime? This is one of the major objections which has been cited and alluded to in the House during the course of this debate.
I should like to place on the record a sample of some of the material I have received in connection with this particular provision especially. I have a letter from Hanmer, Ontario, which reads as follows:
I object very strongly to Bill C-51 for the following reasons.
No way should I have to pay $10 for a firearm's certificate to prove I'm not a criminal or a psycho.
The law-abiding gun owner did not make the criminal or the psycho what he is. It is the government's responsibility to deal with these people and not make it look like it is my fault.
Do you think just because a criminal or a psycho doesn't have a firearm's certificate it will stop him from doing what he had in mind in the first place?
The $10 fee is simply stealing money from law-abiding citizens.
Trying to sneak unacceptable gun legislation through parliament with other possible good legislation is just plain terrible government-pure and simple.
The next letter I should like to quote is from Capreol, Ontario. It reads as follows:
I strongly object to Bill C-51 for the following reasons.
Why should 1 as a law-abiding citizen have to pay $10 for a firearm acquisition certificate just to prove to you that I am not a criminal or that I am not mentally disturbed.
Just because there are some criminals and psychos here in Canada I do not think that it is good government policy to try and penalize every gun-owning Canadian to pay the price for their mistakes.
Why don't you impose stiffer penalties in cases where firearms have been used unlawfully, instead of trying to take the easy way out and treating everyone as a damn criminal?
Do you think that a firearm acquisition certificate will stop a criminal or mentally disturbed person-as in previous school shootings-from committing a crime? No way. Once a person's mind is made up, I am sure that no piece of paper will change it.
The $10 fee is just, in my opinion, plain theft on the part of the government in order to cover part of the cost which the government has spent on several surveys pertaining to firearms in Canada. And how about the employment of people to take these applications for the certificates: who will pay for their wages? Sure it is a $10 fee now, but what will it be next time-$20 or $30?
Also, I would like to say that trying to push through unacceptable gun legislation with other possible good legislation, e.g. wiretapping and parole, is just plain sneaky business on the government's part.
As has been pointed out throughout this debate, the bill has many unacceptable features, but we are only dealing with one here. An assessment of fees in this connection will in no way deter the criminal from obtaining a gun if he is so disposed. What bothers me as we proceed with the passage of various forms of legislation in this House is the tremendous amount of power which is being left in the hands of the governor in council. I am bothered, also, by the tremendous complications which are accumulated as a result of legislation piled upon legislation.
We have reached a time in this country when a lot of the legislation presently on the statute books should be removed. It is time to take a thorough inventory of some of these laws. Our statutes are like accumulated stock. Over the years a business accumulates much dead stock which must be disposed of. This House has been grinding out legislation year after year, and
Criminal Code
this accumulation and proliferation of legislation and regulations has put Canadians in a statutory strait-jacket. It is time to assess our laws, streamline them and scrap those which are either redundant or outdated. It is time to free Canadians of this statutory strait-jacket and take off the hobbles of bureaucracy. It is time the government got off the backs of people.
I hope I have made clear my reasons for finding this bill particularly offensive. Those whom this legislation will govern will be forced to pay a price, to pay a fee which to business people engaged in providing a service will be an additional cost. I hope the minister will approve the amendment which will affect law-abiding citizens whom the legislation should not penalize.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker was perfectly right. This whole cotton-picking provision should not come under the criminal law. Its pith and substance is not that of criminal law. It will merely enable the government to appoint more bureaucrats. Really, the government wants to tax people who get a firearms acquisition certificate and tax the small merchant who sells weapons or ammunition. This new law would punish the innocent, those who have no criminal record and are not criminals. The provision is criminal law in reverse. Those who pay the tax will not be represented; therefore we are contemplating a form of taxation without representation. Instead of telling businessmen who file the various forms and documents the government requires to pay a fee, they should be paid a fee.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Right on.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
I know small merchants are paid for collecting the provincial sales tax. By adopting this provision the government will put an onerous burden on the backs of small businessmen, at the expense of taxpayers. It will set up another bureaucratic empire, with administrators, personnel, and what have you. There will be a deputy in charge of firearms, an assistant deputy, an assistant to the assistant deputy, and so on.
This part of the legislation, at any rate, should not come under the criminal law. Frankly, I think it is ultra vires of this parliament. We should not even be discussing it. The government should bear the cost of the certificates it requires people to file or acquire. The government badgers small business to fill out forms and declarations. Every month Statistics Canada sends out forms. If they are not answered in a few days, you get a note from Ottawa asking why you did not send the information or form. Some people in my constituency were sent forms even after they had gone out of business. They were told to write "not applicable" in the appropriate spaces on the form. My main point is this: parliament has no authrority to pass this legislation. We should not even be discussing this provision.

Motion No. 29.
That bill C-51, to amend the Criminal Code, the Customs Tariff, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act and the Prisons and Reformatories Act, be amended in clause 7 by deleting subclause (1) and substituting the following therefor:
"7.(1) The definition "offence" in section 178.1 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
" "offence", in relation to an authorization or application for an authorization, means an offence or conspiracy to commit an offence described in paragraph (a) and any such offence or conspiracy that there are reasonable grounds to believe has been or may be committed namely,
(a) any offence created by an act of parliament for which an offender may be sentenced to imprisonment for five years or more and any other offence created by an act of parliament for which an offender may be prosecuted by indictment or that is an offence mentioned in section 3 or 20 of the Small Loans Act, that there are reasonable grounds to believe is part of a pattern of criminal activity planned and organized by a number of persons acting in concert in furtherance of the commission of crime involving one or more offences mentioned in paragraph (a) or a conspiracy to commit one or more such offences;"
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
He said: Mr. Speaker, there is an error in motion No. 29. The last words in subparagraph (a) should read, "ten years or more." Perhaps, for clarity, I should read the wording of that part of the amendment as now printed on the order paper. It reads:
(a) any offence created by an act of parliament for which an offender may be sentenced to imprisonment for five years or more.
I seek the unanimous consent of the House to change "five years" to "ten years", so that the last part of the sentence shall read, "to imprisonment for ten years or more". I wonder if the House would consent to that change so that I can debate the motion as amended, not the motion as it presently reads?

I thank hon. members for their consideration in this matter. The reason for the amendment is that as this bill proceeded through committee, a number of amendments were submitted to the offence section of the wiretap bill which listed a variety of offences. The bill enumerated a great variety of specific offences in which case wiretapping is allowed. I think there is consensus amongst the population in favour of wiretapping, but people want it done only in cases of serious offences. The motion before the House which we are submitting states that there should be wiretapping in the case of organized crime, but there should not be wiretapping of little old ladies who have smuggled a pair of panties from Blane, Washington, to Vancouver. I see the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) looking incredulous. I thought she might, so 1 took the trouble of bringing in section 192 of the Customs Act. I use just that example, but there are a number of other examples of extremely minor offences which are common occurrences, actually just slips on the part of the population but for which wiretapping is allowed.
Under section 192 of the Customs Act, any person who smuggles anything valued at less than $200 is subject to the forfeiture of that item or a one-year jail term. If there is a decline in respect for law and order, it is a disease of the body politic .. . He said:
I come not to give advice but to express my impressions of the experience of your neighbour to the south. I come because I desperately hope to see from nations in this world the new moral leadership that is founded on the proposition that governments can protect their people without acting unfairly or immorally themselves in any respect. I believe that. I do not believe the rule of law can be an effective means of social change otherwise. We can have law and order, and we can have the forces of law and order obey the law. Perhaps I might just say a word at this point. I appreciate the fact that two hon. members have spoken across the range of the wiretap section. They have spoken briefly and I know there is a desire to move very quickly, so I shall be brief. I might say, first of all, that I do not think much is accomplished by one group or by another group, whether on this side of the House or on the other, claiming that they are more concerned with civil liberties than some other group in the House. I think all groups and all members of the House are concerned with the rights and civil liberties of Canadians, since this is obviously a function of parliament. But we need to address ourselves to the problems which face the country, and it is up to us to deal with them in a realistic and proper way while at the same time protecting Canadians.
This having been said, I want to go briefly into the history of the wiretapping section which was put into the Criminal Code in 1974 after long discussion, debate and examination of the question by a parliamentary committee. That committee came to a number of conclusions. Until then, as hon. members know, there was no law relating to electronic surveillance or wiretapping. There was no law prohibiting it. It was clear there were people engaged in private wiretapping and that the police were also engaged in wiretapping without any judicial supervision whatsoever.
The committee, in 1974, came to three conclusions. First, that there should be no private wiretapping-that no private citizen should be able to eavesdrop on the telephone or communications of another citizen. That is the law now, and will remain the law and should remain the law. There is no dispute about that. Second, the committee came to the conclusion that electronic surveillance was an indispensable tool in the hands of the police against a certain set of crimes, and that under
Criminal Code
proper judicial supervision electronic surveillance should be available to the police for this purpose.
Furthermore, there should be a particular section in the act relating to organized crime which was, and is, a menace in this country. The particular wording in the Criminal Code related to organized crime was written by Ron Atkey, a former member of parliament who sat for the Conservative party, a man whose record in civil liberties is well recognized but who, in parliament, acknowledged that in certain circumstances wiretapping was necessary. He, in fact, wrote the wording relating to organized crime.
Two things have happened since 1974 when that law was written. One is that the organized crime section has not worked because no judge knows the legal meaning of "organized crime". The other is that every attorney general in this country has annually reported that because of the provisions of the wiretap legislation they are handicapped in the investigation of certain major crimes and handicapped in their investigation of organized crime. I submit, as I have submitted throughout, that there is no dispute in this country or, at any rate, there should not be, as to who feels the greater concern for the civil liberties of Canadians. But I also assert that it is the responsibility of the House to take account of the reports we have received on the activities of organized crime and endeavour to write the law in such a way as to give the police, under proper judicial supervision, the instruments to allow them to investigate, charge, prosecute and convict organized criminals more effectively.
What went on in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs was a long and thorough investigation of that section. Knowledgeable people from both sides of the House served on that committee. I had initially suggested to the committee that an authorization for wiretap should be obtainable by the police from a judge for any offence carrying a sentence of five years or more. After much discussion, that proposition was rejected by the committee and the committee went back to the form of the existing Criminal Code, working on the basis of a list of serious crimes with a separate section on organized crime. So if the police officers, through Crown counsel, went to a judge they could get an authorization on the basis of the suspected commission of named offences or of organized criminal activities. The committee examined that list, the list presently in the Criminal Code.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the minister is anxious to proceed with his legislation, and I may be able to save some time. He is now referring to a section of the motion which deals with the definition of "organized crime" and the offences which are tappable. From reading my section, I now see what the minister is getting at. I can assure the House that I did not intend to limit the tapping of organized crime as defined in the motion only to those offences which carry a sentence of ten years or more. I intended to leave it open to any other offence created by an act of parliament for which an offender may be prosecuted by indictment; that is, an offence mentioned in section 3 or section 20 of the Small Loans Act. So it is inadvertence on my part, and for that I apologize to the House.
As I say, if the Minister of Justice wants to save time, it is not necessary for him to dwell on that section. My intention is very clear; I want this section to have the capacity to tap organized crime for all indictable offences, including, of course, the sections under the Small Loans Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE

Mr. Speaker, I asked the hon. member to listen to me for a moment, and I am glad that he did and that he got my point. Because by the use of the words "in furtherance" in his amendment, it clearly has the result that the only way you can wiretap organized crime is if an offence on the list was being committed-which leaves out certain serious offences and would be, as I say, an open season for organized crime. I accept the word of the hon. member that that is a case

of inadvertence, but obviously it leaves me having to resist the amendment.
Even forgetting the organized crime section for a moment, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that some of the offences that I have mentioned are serious. They are not necessarily committed by what might be called organized crime; they are committed by major criminals and should be in the list of offences for which the police, under proper judicial supervision, can obtain an authorization to wiretap.
I mention only the last one, pornography, which the committee put in deliberately. There is a good deal of concern in this House and in the country about the kind of hard core pornography that is coming into Canada. I am not referring to the Playboy magazine type, but to hard core pornography, depicting young children in the commission of sexual acts either with themselves or with adults, bestiality and other magazines of that kind. It seems to me that the committee looked at these offences carefully, examined each one and made a recommendation to the House which should, with respect, be accepted.
One last quick point, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member referred to smuggling. He ridiculed the section on the basis of some tourist coming in with some panties which she refused to declare. I can assure the House, as I did the committee, that the customs officials have neither the intention nor the resources to wiretap in those cases. Whether or not it be someone failing to declare a pair of panties, the section also includes smuggling carloads or truckloads of, for example, pornographic material. It includes smuggling of stolen goods in huge quantities by very sophisticated, major criminals. Therefore, it seems to me that while one might ridicule smuggling on the one hand, there are certainly smuggling activites which are serious and dangerous and are a large part of criminal activity in this country.

Mr. Speaker, my summer is moving along just as quickly as that of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). I should like to stroll the streets of Prince George to be with my constituents just as much as the minister would like to walk down Robson's Cross in Vancouver and do the same there. His need, of course, is greater than mine because I am not the sponsor of this bill which is before us and which is cutting into the work we should be doing in our constituencies this year.
I sat on this committee for some time as a layman, and as you can well imagine, Mr. Speaker, the deliberations were often tedious and boring for a layman who does not understand all this legal jargon which our learned and honourable colleagues indulge in at times in this House and certainly in committee. But as a private citizen and a layman, I was appalled, concerned, at times frightened, by the testimony that was placed before the committee.
Not all the evidence was brought before the committee, of course, because when the committee was finally prorogued on the gun sections of the bill I understand there were some 24 application from groups of individuals throughout the county to appear before the committee to give testimony. I never
